tiles.title: Login
tiles.opener: Who uses it: every user, before anything else — the first screen and, for anyone who forgets a password, a recurring one. What "done" looks like: signed in, or told exactly why not without leaking which part was wrong. The one screen every ERP app has and the one where getting the details wrong locks real users out. Composed entirely from existing components, zero new CSS: .bo-widget (the card primitive) centers the form on the canvas, fields are plain .bo-form-fields with the correct autocomplete tokens (username / current-password — this is what lets password managers fill the form), and errors use the same validation-summary pattern as any other form. Try it: submit the empty form. Not for re-authentication mid-task — when a workspace needs a step-up credential check without abandoning the screen the user was on (confirming a destructive action, re-entering a password after a session timeout), a full-page navigation throws away that context; use a dialog carrying the same two fields instead. This page is for the one navigation every session starts with, not an interruption inside one.

Invalid credentials
one generic message — never "no such user" (account enumeration)
Account locked
a distinct message with the unlock path; do NOT reuse the invalid-credentials copy

Submitting

No JS

the live demo form carries novalidate, which turns off the browser's own constraint validation — with no initValidationSummary() to call checkValidity() either, Submit fires with empty required fields unvalidated and the summary box never appears; the canonical form in the Markup section below omits novalidate, so a real deployment of it would fall back to native browser validation bubbles instead of losing validation entirely

the form, carrying the post-login destination in a hidden field

tiles.title: Error pages
tiles.opener: Who uses it: every user, eventually — a stale bookmark, a link shared before a record moved, a permission that changed since yesterday, a request that failed server-side. How often: rare per user, universal per app — every ERP hits all three of 404, 403 and 500 sooner or later. What "done" looks like: the reader is never at a dead end — one clear sentence for what happened, and at least one real place to go next. Three status codes, ONE shape: icon, title, description, actions — .bo-state and .bo-state--error, already shipped, nothing new. Not for a section failing to load inside a page you're still on — a table or panel that can't fetch its own data is .bo-state--error used inline, right where the section was, with the rest of the screen still usable. This pattern is for when the NAVIGATION itself failed, not one region of a page that otherwise worked.
states: Full navigation (404/403/500 at the URL)
this page's own shape, canvas-centered, real HTTP status
Inside a fragment swap
the identical .bo-state--error markup sized to the swap target — a table that fails to load shows this INSIDE itself, the rest of the screen stays usable
500, retryable
Retry is the primary action; a repeat failure shows the same page again rather than a different, more alarming one — consistency over escalation
404 / 403, not retryable
no Retry button at all — offering one for a resource that is genuinely gone or genuinely not yours is a false promise, not politeness
Not authenticated, vs. authenticated-but-forbidden
two different things a 403 must never conflate: a signed-out visitor gets redirected to login, never this page; THIS page is only for a signed-in user whose role genuinely lacks the permission
No JS
fully functional — every element here is a plain link or the browser's own navigation; nothing on this page depends on JS running at all
dataContract: GET /pos/:id (missing)
a real 404, full HTML page — never a 200 with "not found" text; a search engine, a monitoring probe and a browser's own error handling all key off the status line, not the copy
GET /pos/:id (no access)
a real 403, same page shape, the permission-specific copy
any request, server fault
a real 500; the copy never guesses at a cause the server doesn't actually know
an htmx fragment request that 404s/403s/500s

the SAME .bo-state--error markup, sized for the swap target rather than the whole viewport — the shape doesn't change, only its container does. htmx discards non-2xx by default; the swap target must opt in via htmx:beforeSwap the same way any other 4xx/5xx content this framework documents does

tiles.title: App frame
tiles.opener: Who uses it: everyone, on every screen — the persistent chrome the whole suite lives inside. How often: it never leaves the screen. What "done" looks like: any module is one click away, and search, notifications and the user menu are in the same place on every screen of every module. The anatomy is the modern consensus across enterprise suites (Fiori's shell bar, Dynamics' area-plus-sitemap, Lightning, Carbon's UI shell): a suite-level top bar, a module-level sidebar, and a main region that belongs entirely to the page. Not for a single-task dedicated device — a handheld scanner runs RF full-screen with no frame at all; and not an iframe — the frame is the layout every page renders inside, not a container that embeds pages.

the sidebar's active entry carries aria-current="page" + the visible marker — two channels
Narrow (<900px shell width)
the sidebar collapses to its icon rail; labels stay in the accessibility tree. A bottom-nav tier is deliberately NOT shipped — re-opens on a real consumer need
No permission for a module
absent from switcher and sidebar both — a disabled module teaches nothing and leaks structure

no badge, no error — the bar never fails loudly over a number

No JS

the switcher and user menus are native popover — they open, close on Escape/click-away and return focus with zero JS; only menu anchoring (initDropdowns) is an enhancement. Search submits as a form; every module link is a real link

tiles.title: Suite home
tiles.opener: Who uses it: anyone whose work spans modules — a controller touching Finance and Purchasing, an ops lead across Warehouse and Reports; the screen behind the brand link and the switcher's "home". How often: between tasks, and first thing after sign-in when no single role owns the day. What "done" looks like: cross-module status in one glance, and any module one click away — the sidebar at this level lists modules, not one module's screens (the Fiori "My Home" / Dynamics areas shape). Not for one role's daily queue — a buyer who lives in Purchasing all day wants role home, which shows their work, not the suite; and not just a launcher — a pure tile grid with no live status is app launch.

tiles.title: App launch
tiles.opener: Who uses it: anyone opening the suite, every session — the first screen after sign-in. What "done" looks like: the right app is one tap away, whether it's a favourite or three deep in a category. A suite entry screen — the icon-grid launcher (the "Bento UI" / tablet-launcher archetype from the device-coverage table — same .bo-widget-grid container-query mechanism as a dashboard, at a smaller tile size, not a new grid component). Tiles are plain links composed into .bo-widget cards with real CSS icons (themable currentColor glyphs) where a glyph is genuinely right, an initials chip where none is, and inline <svg> where a tenant brings their own; the category row is the ordinary tabs pattern; a "folder" tile is just a widget whose body holds a cluster of small tiles. Zero new CSS. Not for returning a user to a specific record they already know — a bookmark, a notification, or a saved link should land directly on the object page or the list report, never route back through the launcher grid to get there.

tiles.title: Role home
tiles.opener: Who uses it: every named role — a buyer, an approver, a warehouse supervisor — each seeing their own version. How often: the first screen after sign-in, and the one they come back to between tasks. What "done" looks like: the reader knows in one glance whether anything needs them, and leaves for the screen that resolves it. Not a launcher — a tile grid of every app someone could open is app launch; this shows live content about their work. And not a dashboard: the reporting dashboard monitors the business (is the period on track), a role home monitors my work (is anything waiting on me). Same widgets, different subject — and confusing the two is how a home screen turns into a chart wall nobody acts on.

per-role content

tiles.title: Command bar
tiles.opener: Who uses it: power users who know what they want — a dispatcher jumping to PO-88213, a controller running "post period" — without walking the menu. How often: dozens of times a day, which is why it is keyboard-first and why the shortcut must never be stolen from the browser. What "done" looks like: they typed a few characters and the screen they wanted is open, hands never leaving the keyboard. Not a replacement for navigation — it rewards people who already know the name of the thing. A first-time or occasional user needs the visible structure of app launch, and a user narrowing an unknown set needs the filter panel; a command bar answers neither.

tiles.title: List report
tiles.opener: Who uses it: AP clerks, all day — the screen they live in. What "done" looks like: find the invoices that need action, act on them in bulk, and never lose your place. Composed entirely from shipped components; the data table page documents the table itself, this page documents the screen. Not for a single record's full detail — once a clerk opens one invoice to review or act on it alone, that screen is a record detail (or an object page for a richer one); list-report's job stops at finding and bulk-acting on rows, not deep-diving into one.

tiles.title: Advanced filter panel
tiles.opener: The filter set that outgrew the bar. A finance or purchasing user opens the same list a dozen times a day and narrows it a different way each time — cost centre, status, date range, amount band. They do not want twelve controls permanently across the top; they want the two they use constantly visible and the rest a click away. "Done" means the list reloads and what is currently filtering it stays visible after the panel closes — a filter you cannot see is a filter you will forget you set, and then mistrust the numbers. Not for a list with one obvious narrowing dimension — a single search box or a two-option status filter is already inline in the list report's own bar; reach for the grouped, chip-backed panel here only once distinct facets pile up (cost centre, date band, status, and more), not by default for every list.

tiles.title: Value help
tiles.opener: Who uses it: anyone typing a code they cannot remember — a buyer picking a material out of forty thousand, a clerk choosing a cost centre; dozens of times a day, inside a form they are part-way through. What "done" looks like: the right code is in the field, and the reader is back where they were with nothing else lost. The picker is a detour, not a destination — which is why choosing must put focus back in the field they were filling, not leave it at the top of the document. Not when the option set is small — a couple dozen fixed choices belong in a plain native select, not a dialog with search and paging behind it. This pattern is for the case a select cannot handle: a list too large to enumerate in one control.

tiles.title: Object page
tiles.opener: A long record, navigated in sections instead of scrolled as one feed. Who uses it: whoever owns one record end to end — a buyer opening a PO, an approver checking it before signing; many times a day, one object at a time. What "done" looks like: the reader can see the object's status without scrolling, reach any section in one click, and act on it from anywhere on the page. The long-record counterpart to record detail: same content, but too tall to take in at once, so it gains navigation of its own. Not for a record you can take in at one glance — the anchor rail and sticky action bar are overhead you only earn by being long. That one is record detail.

tiles.title: Record detail
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever owns this record, checking its status or adding to its history — a buyer, an approver, anyone who clicked in from a list row. How often: every time a list row is opened — this is the default landing for "tell me about this one," many times a day across a team. What "done" looks like: the current state is read in one glance, without opening anything else. The composed detail screen behind any list row: record cards, a status timeline, and an audit trail stacked in a feed — all standard components, generic to any ERP. This example is a purchase order; the shape is the same for an invoice, a change request, or a leave request. Not once the record stops fitting in one scan — when a reader has to hunt for a section, it wants anchor navigation and a sticky action bar, which is object page. Same content, different reading problem.

tiles.title: Master-detail
tiles.opener: M2 of the four data-maintenance patterns (and the most common one in practice): a list of records, and clicking a row opens that record's fields in a panel beside the list or a dialog over it. A back-office user uses this all day — find the vendor, fix two fields, move on — and "done" means the list stays put, keeping their scroll position, filters and sort, while only the detail changes. Not when one record deserves the whole screen — the split exists so a user can move ALONG the list without losing their place; if they are working one record end to end, the panel is just a narrower object page.

Stale data

No permission for a metric

the result region says so plainly ("Choose parameters and run") — never an empty table that looks like a zero result
Running

Empty result
"No open items for CC-4021 in 2026-07" — the parameters restated, because an empty report is a finding and the reader must see what was asked
Too many rows
state the cap and offer the export ("12,480 rows — showing the first 500; export for all"); never silently truncate
Parameter error
422 re-renders the form with field messages; the PREVIOUS result stays on screen, clearly still labelled with its own run-line
Stale result
parameters edited but not re-run → the result keeps its original run-line; a figure never re-labels itself with inputs that did not produce it
No JS

long runs

tiles.title: Issued document
tiles.opener: Who uses it: nobody, on screen — this is the artefact the ERP emits: a purchase order sent to a vendor, an invoice, a delivery note travelling with goods. How often: every time a document is issued, usually unattended. What "done" looks like: a page a stranger can read without your system — sender, recipient, document number, lines, totals, terms — that survives pagination and a black-and-white printer. Not a screen, and not a PDF engine — if a person needs to work with the record, that is the object page; and rendering the actual PDF is your server's job (see the grill verdict below), not this framework's.
states: Draft
the word DRAFT in the document identity block and in a print-only line — never a colour wash or a watermark image, which a black-and-white printer or a forced-colors reader loses entirely
Issued
issue date present; the document is the record of what was sent
Copy / re-issue
marked in text with the re-issue date beside the original
Cancelled
stated in words at the top; the lines stay readable because a cancelled document still has to be auditable
Multi-page
header and totals repeat; parties and terms blocks never split; the print-only continuation line carries the document number so a loose page is identifiable
No lines
refuse to emit — a document with no lines is a bug upstream, not an empty state to style
No JS

fully functional — this page has no JS dependency; it's a rendered, printable document (the initScanInput() mentioned here belongs to the separate goods-receipt screen that later reads its barcode, not to this page)
dataContract: GET /po/:id/document

this HTML, standalone (no app shell, no nav) — a complete page your renderer or a browser can print directly. 404 if the record does not exist; 5xx if rendering itself fails — both as a plain error page, never a broken document that LOOKS complete
GET /po/:id/document.pdf
your server runs the SAME HTML through its renderer; the PDF and the printed page cannot disagree because they are one source
issue / re-issue
a re-issued document states it ("Copy · re-issued 24 Aug 2026") — an unmarked duplicate of a financial document is a control failure
draft
a document that is not yet issued must SAY so on its face (see states) — never render a draft that looks issued

wrongChoice.clause: Not a screen, and not a PDF engine

tiles.title: Notification
tiles.opener: Who uses it: anyone whose work finishes while they are not watching — a posting run, an export, an approval granted upstream. How often: glanced at many times a day, read fully a few. What "done" looks like: the unread count is zero because each item was seen and either dismissed or followed. This is the surface for things that happened; it never blocks on you. Not for work that needs your action — a row that blocks on a person belongs in the inbox, not here; and not for things happening while you watch — that is an alert or toast's moment. The grill that settled the shape (101.5): it is BOTH a navbar glance and a screen — the bell dropdown shows the latest few, the screen holds the readable history — and both compose from shipped pieces.
states: Empty
"No notifications" — plain, not celebratory; unlike the inbox, an empty history is not an achievement
Unread present
the bell badge carries the count; each unread item carries the worded badge — two channels at both levels
All read
bell badge absent (not "0" — a zero badge reads as noise); items keep their "read" byline
Dead record
text kept, link removed, stated plainly ("no longer exists") with dismiss as the only action
Very long history
paginate at the screen level (load-more); the dropdown never grows beyond its few
No JS

the bell opens its menu via native popovertarget (Popover API), so browsing notifications still works; "Mark read" and "Dismiss" are bare type="button" elements with no script or form wired to them on this page, so they do nothing — and the bell's live-count poll (hx-trigger="every 60s", described in Data contract) needs htmx's own script to run at all
dataContract: GET /notifications

the list fragment + the unread count for the bell badge; each item carries data-notification-id and data-unread so an agent reads state without scraping prose. On 5xx/timeout: the bell keeps its last-known count and the dropdown shows an inline retry — never a blank menu, since "I don't know" and "you have zero" read as the same thing to a glancing reader
POST /notifications/:id/read
the item re-rendered read + the new count; idempotent — a second post returns the same state, never an error
POST /notifications/:id/dismiss
204, item removed on next fetch; dismissing an already-dismissed item is 204 too
arrival
new items appear on the next poll (hx-trigger="every 60s" on the bell count is enough); the SCREEN never reorders under a reader mid-scroll

wrongChoice.clause: Not for work that needs your action

tiles.title: Job monitor
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever is accountable when unattended work fails — an integrations admin, an ops lead, the person the inbox assigned an exception to. How often: a glance most days, a deep look the moment something is late. What "done" looks like: every scheduled job shows its last result and next run, and nothing has failed silently. Not for authoring schedules — cron expressions, dependency chains and retry policy are your ERP's admin module; this screen is scoped to monitoring jobs someone already scheduled — view, retry, cancel, nothing that changes what runs next time. And not the place to read one run's own numbers: a finished job links to its own result (a report or a staging screen); this page only tracks whether runs happened and how they went.
states: Running
warning badge + aria-busy="true" on the cell, elapsed time, not a spinner alone
Failed
danger badge + when; Retry is the row's action; the failure REASON belongs one click away, not crammed into the cell
Stalled
distinct from running — same warning tone, but the word changes and the duration is shown; a job announcing nothing for an hour is not the same as one announcing progress
Succeeded
success badge + a link to the run's own result; the monitor never shows the result inline
Never run
plain muted text, not a badge — a badge implies something happened
No jobs scheduled
"No scheduled jobs" — genuinely rare in a live ERP, but the empty state still has to say something, not render a bare header row
No JS

the table itself reads fine as static markup, but Retry/Cancel are bare type="button" elements with no script or form wired to them on this page, so they do nothing — and the row's own polling (hx-trigger="every 30s", described in Data contract) needs htmx's own script to run at all, so a running/stalled job's status never advances without a manual reload
dataContract: GET /jobs
the row fragment; each row carries data-job-id and data-status (running/failed/succeeded/stalled/never-run) so an agent reads state without parsing badge text
POST /jobs/:id/retry
the row re-rendered running; 409 if it is already running — re-render with the current state, never queue a second attempt silently
POST /jobs/:id/cancel
the row re-rendered with its last completed state; a job that cannot be cancelled mid-step says so rather than appearing to stop
polling
hx-trigger="every 30s" on the table while any row is running or stalled; polling stops once nothing is in flight — an idle screen has no reason to keep asking

wrongChoice.clause: Not for authoring schedules

tiles.title: Schedule calendar
tiles.opener: A planner or supervisor scans a month for what is booked — deliveries, maintenance windows, shift cover — several times a day during a busy week, and once a day otherwise. "Done" is picking a day and seeing exactly what is on it without losing the month underneath, the same swap discipline master-detail uses for a list and a record. Not for authoring a schedule — creating, moving or cancelling entries is the admin module's job, not this screen's — and not for one entry's own detail or history, which belongs to record detail, not a month grid. This page only answers "what is on this day".
states: Nothing selected
the panel holds a one-line prompt ("Pick a day to see what's on it"), not a blank box
Loading the day
aria-busy on the panel only; the month stays interactive so the reader can pick a different day mid-load
Empty day
a day that IS a link (server said it has entries) but returns none by the time it's opened — say so, do not show an empty table with headers and nothing under them
Non-working day opened via a bookmark
the DIFFERENT empty — explain it is a closed/holiday date, not "nothing scheduled yet"
Conflict on one entry
flagged in the row with a badge (see the demo above), not surfaced as a page-level error — the other entries that day are still fine
No permission to open a day's detail
the day stays a plain cell rather than a disabled-looking link — a control a reader can see but never use is worse than one that is simply absent
Narrow screen

panel and grid stack in source order — the split's own auto-fit grid (see .sched-split below) collapses to one column below ~36rem; the calendar component itself carries no container breakpoint, nothing new to build here
No JS

fully functional — this page has no JS dependency; each day is a real <a href="#schedule-detail"> fragment link (native anchor navigation, no script), and the page imports no @busy-office/ui/js behavior
dataContract: GET /schedule?month=2026-08
the month grid, with each day's data-day mark and whether it is a link baked in server-side; the detail panel renders empty until a day is chosen
GET /schedule/day/:date
the day-detail fragment only, swapped into #schedule-detail. Never re-render the month — that is what loses the reader's place in it
404 / day now empty
an entry was cancelled after the month rendered — replace the panel with an empty state naming the day, and stop treating that cell as a link on the next month fetch
GET /schedule/day/:date on a closed or holiday date

wrongChoice.clause: Not for authoring a schedule

tiles.title: Settings & admin
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a workspace admin, occasionally a first-time setup wizard. How often: rarely per person, but every workspace has one. What "done" looks like: a section's values saved, or an unsaved change clearly marked before the admin navigates away. Composed entirely from existing components — .bo-tabs to split General/Users/Notifications, .bo-form-section fieldsets, .bo-checkbox for on/off preferences (there is no separate "switch" component — a labeled checkbox already covers the same setting, per the "one component, many settings" principle), and the data table for the user list. One person editing their own notification or display preferences needs none of that surface; use a plain detail form scoped to that person instead.

a success alert in the section, not a global toast — the user needs to know WHICH section saved
Unsaved changes
a dirty marker in the save bar; warn on section switch, not just on unload
Validation error
field-level messages; focus the first invalid control
Read-only (non-admin)
render values as key-value facts and omit the save bar
Destructive action (not in this demo)
confirm dialog naming the exact consequence and requiring the object name typed for irreversible ones
No JS

the section form with current values

POST /settings/:section/reset
defaults restored — behind a confirm dialog, never a bare button

wrongChoice.clause: Not for a single end user's own preferences

tiles.title: RF task menu

An RF device runs a handful of tasks per shift, not a suite — this menu stays that short on purpose (roadmap 109.7).

tiles render immediately with a skeleton count; never block the whole grid on one slow endpoint
Zero open
the tile stays, badge reads 0 — see Count above; a vanished tile reads as "not my job today," which is wrong
Session lost

Cached menus and stale-data cues are an APP/infrastructure layer (the reference products sell session persistence as a server product) — this framework ships the visuals a reconnect needs, and promises nothing it does not ship
Permission-scoped

No JS
fully functional — this page has no JS dependency; each tile is a real <a href> (native navigation to the task queue), and the page imports no @busy-office/ui/js behavior

one entry per task type with its open count; 401 → redirect to login, never a silent empty menu
GET /rf/tasks/:type

wrongChoice.clause: Not for

tiles.title: RF task queue
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a warehouse floor worker after picking a task from the RF task menu — "what's next" for that task type. What "done" looks like: the worker reads top-to-bottom, taps the top row, and starts working it — no cross-referencing between columns. Not for editing a line's data on this screen — see Editable, refused below. states: Loading
a skeleton row set at the same spacious row height, so the tap targets don't jump once data lands
Empty — nothing queued
"All caught up" text plus a link back to the task menu, not a bare blank table
Empty — filtered out
N/A on this screen — the queue has no filter control; filtering happens by picking a different task type from the menu
Claim conflict (409)
the row is removed from this worker's queue with a brief alert; no destructive retry
Session lost

the reconnect state: the queue re-renders as the server has it, and a claim attempted while the link was down is simply retried — claiming is idempotent server-side (the 409 row above). Offline caching is infrastructure, not a screen promise
No JS
fully functional — this page has no JS dependency; the demo has no button or script wired to it at all, and it imports no @busy-office/ui/js behavior
dataContract: GET /rf/tasks/:type
the ordered queue, next-up first; 204 for an empty queue
POST /rf/tasks/:id/claim
marks the task in-progress and returns the detail screen route; 409 if another worker already claimed it — re-render the queue, don't just retry

wrongChoice.clause: Not for

tiles.title: Goods receipt (RF scanner)
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a warehouse floor worker, one-handed and often gloved, holding a scanner instead of a mouse. What "done" looks like: every expected line accounted for — received in full, received partial, or explicitly not received — before the receipt posts. A GR (goods receipt) screen driven by a handheld RF scanner — the scanner types the barcode fast and sends Enter, so the field needs to stay focused and clear itself between scans. Composed from data-scan-input (new opt-in behavior, no new CSS — a plain .bo-input), the existing .bo-quantity at data-density="spacious" for a warehouse-floor large target, and the data table for the receiving log. A visually-hidden aria-live="polite" region (linked via the field's own aria-describedby) announces each successful scan — a screen-reader/low-vision RF user gets non-visual confirmation without it being read for every sighted user. Not for a desk-based receiving clerk keying a paper packing slip. Without a physical scanner there is no barcode to feed the always-focused field, the spacious steppers just waste screen space, and the workflow is really "type these numbers in and check them" — that's a detail form at normal density, not this pattern.
states: Waiting for scan
the field holds focus permanently; every state change must return focus to it
Unknown barcode
an alert plus an audible or visible cue — the user is looking at the goods, not the screen
Over-receipt
a warning with the tolerance stated; block only past the policy limit
Partial receipt
the line shows received/ordered; posting a partial is normal and must not warn
Complete
a clear terminal state — the next scan starts a NEW receipt rather than silently appending
Session lost / flaky wifi

the RECONNECT state: on regaining the server, re-render as the server has it. Session persistence is INFRASTRUCTURE (the reference products sell it as a server), not a screen promise — an unsent scan is retyped, which is honest and cheaper than a silently dropped one that reads as saved
No JS

the scan field, quantity input, and table render as plain, focusable, typable native controls, but the core flow cannot complete: initScanInput() is what listens for the terminator key, clears/refocuses the field, and dispatches bo:scan — without it, pressing Enter after a scan does nothing, so no line ever reaches the log. The +/− quantity steppers also need initQuantity(), though the number input itself stays usable via keyboard/typing
dataContract: POST /receipts/:id/scan
the matched line fragment with its updated count; 404 → an unknown-barcode alert that does NOT steal focus from the scan field
POST /receipts/:id
the posted receipt; 422 for over-receipt beyond tolerance
GET /receipts/:id
resume a partially entered receipt — warehouse sessions get interrupted

wrongChoice.clause: Not for a desk-based receiving clerk keying a paper packing slip.

tiles.title: RF picking
tiles.opener: Who uses it: a picker with a gun in one hand and the other on the rack — the highest-volume RF activity in any warehouse. How often: hundreds of times a shift, one task line at a time. What "done" looks like: right bin confirmed by scan, right item confirmed by scan, quantity entered without taking gloves off, and the next line already on screen. The screen answers before the worker asks — task, bin, item, quantity — in the KV header every RF screen here shares. Not for checking stock without moving it — counting what a bin holds is the count pattern, which is blind by design; picking knows exactly what it wants and verifies the worker found it.
states: Awaiting bin scan
the field names what it expects; the header carries the bin as text — the scan is confirmation, not discovery
Wrong bin / wrong item
error flash + the reason in the live region; the field clears and refocuses for the retry
Short pick
Report short opens the reason path; the line completes with its shortfall recorded, never silently adjusted
Line re-assigned (409)
who took it, then the next line — flow beats blame
Queue empty
back to the task menu; an empty pick screen teaches nothing
Session lost
the RECONNECT state: on regaining the server, re-render the line as the server has it. Session persistence is infrastructure, not a screen promise
No JS
the form still posts on Enter (the wedge's terminator) and the server re-renders with the verdict — the flash and keypad are enhancements; the KV header, field and bar are markup
dataContract: GET /rf/pick/next
the next task line — this screen, server-rendered; an empty queue returns the task-menu redirect, never a blank pick screen
POST /rf/pick/:line/confirm
bin + item + qty; 422 names WHICH check failed (wrong bin / wrong item / qty over need) so the worker fixes one thing, not everything
POST … short (qty < need)
requires a reason code (select) — a silent short is tomorrow's stock discrepancy
409 on a re-assigned line
re-render with who took it and the NEXT line — the worker keeps moving, never argues with a screen

wrongChoice.clause: Not for checking stock without moving it

tiles.title: RF putaway
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever moves what receiving just accepted into its storage bin — the second half of every inbound delivery. How often: per handling unit, all day while trucks unload. What "done" looks like: the HU physically in the bin the system chose, proven by scanning that bin's label — the verification idiom: the screen names the destination in bold, and the scan must match it. A wrong bin flashes red before the pallet is set down, which is precisely when a putaway error is still free to fix. Not the receiving step — goods receipt captures what ARRIVED against the PO; putaway moves what receipt accepted. Merging them makes dock workers do binning decisions with a truck waiting, which is how both jobs end up done badly.
states: Awaiting verification
destination bold in the header; the field names it again in its label
Wrong bin scanned
error flash + expected bin announced; field clears for retry — the pallet is still on the truck of the forklift, where the fix is free
Confirmed
badge + text, then the next HU; the flash alone is never the record
Bin full
the exception button, not a freehand override — the server picks the alternative
Session lost
reconnect re-renders the HU as the server has it; persistence is infrastructure, not a screen promise
No JS
Enter posts the scan; the server's re-render carries the verdict. Header, field and bar are markup
dataContract: GET /rf/putaway/next
the next HU + its system-chosen bin, server-rendered
POST /rf/putaway/:hu/confirm
the scanned bin; the server RE-CHECKS the match (the client compare is UX, never the control) and returns the next HU
POST … bin-full
returns an alternative bin for the same HU — the worker never chooses a bin freehand
409 (bin occupied since assignment)
a new destination with the reason — never a silent reroute; reroutes without reasons are audit holes

wrongChoice.clause: Not the receiving step

tiles.title: RF count
tiles.opener: Who uses it: whoever walks the aisles for a physical inventory or a cycle count. How often: cycle counts daily on a rotation; wall-to-wall counts a few times a year, all hands. What "done" looks like: the bin scanned open, what is ACTUALLY there entered, submitted — and critically, the expected quantity was never on screen. A count is blind by design: show the book figure and the counter anchors to it, and the count stops measuring reality and starts confirming the record. That single fact shapes this screen — it is the one RF header that deliberately withholds a number. Not for correcting a quantity you already know is wrong — a known discrepancy is a stock adjustment with a reason, made at a desk on the record; a count is how you FIND discrepancies, not how you fix them.
states: Awaiting bin scan
the count stays closed until the right bin opens it — counting the wrong bin is worse than not counting
Counting
quantity empty (not zero); Submit disabled until a figure exists — empty and 0 are different facts
Recount demanded
the same position re-opens, SAID to be a recount — a silent recount reads as a glitch and gets pencil-whipped
Item not found
its own exception, not a typed 0 — zero-with-reason and counted-zero diverge in the variance report
Session lost
reconnect re-renders the position as the server has it; an uncommitted count is retyped — honest, and cheaper than a wrong committed one
No JS
scan posts on Enter, the count is a plain form; flash and steppers are enhancements
dataContract: GET /rf/count/next
the next bin/item to count — WITHOUT the book quantity; blindness is enforced server-side, not by the screen's good manners
POST /rf/count/:pos/submit
the counted figure; a large variance may return a RECOUNT of the same position (the server decides the threshold), announced as such
POST … item-not-found
records a zero-with-reason — distinct from a typed 0, which is a counted empty bin
409 (position already counted)
who counted it and the next position — double-counting is noise in the variance report

wrongChoice.clause: Not for correcting a quantity you already know is wrong
